confirmed: Read the complete NIH author manuscript XML, including references and Figure 1 caption, through NCBI E-utilities (db=pmc&id=11065427); no PDF was obtainable. Metadata confirms NIHMS1959465, the title/authors, J Creat Behav 58(1), 128-136, and electronic publication on 11 January 2024 (article/front/article-meta).

ai_vs_human, context_class = ai_vs_human, core = no, criterion_1 = not_met, and criterion_3 = met are correct. Randomized prompt order and random selection of stories for raters do not assign people to AI assistance (Methods S1/P7-P9; Creativity Assessment S2/P10).

The manuscript reports 50 Prolific writers aged 18-35, all native English speakers, supplying six stories each: 300 human stories. GPT-3 supplied 300 stories and GPT-4 supplied 120 replication stories. These are collected counts; no people-randomized count or explicit final writer count is supplied (Methods S1/P7-P9; Statistical Analyses S5/P14).

The task used three cue words, about five sentences, six prompts in randomized order, and five minutes per human story. The GPT-3 engine is called davinci-003; temperature was sampled from .65-.80, with frequency and presence penalties each set to 1 (Methods S1/P8-P9).

The manuscript states 240 independent Prolific raters, 12 ratings per story, a 1-5 scale, and 30 stories per rater; GPT-4 supplied one rating per story. It does not reconcile this allocation across the original and additional GPT-4 corpora (Creativity Assessment S2/P10-P11).

S1-O1's reported values are exact: human minus GPT-3 β = .07, 95% CI [−0.02, 0.16], t = 1.59, p = .11; R2 = .39. The source explicitly interprets this as 0.07 creativity points for the same length and prompt (Results, paragraph 3, S6/P17).

S1-O2's reported values and its caveat are exact: pooled human-rated comparisons give GPT-3 t = −1.66, p = .10 and GPT-4 t = 1.98, p = .05. The source calls both tendencies lower and nonsignificant despite printing a positive GPT-4 t; the checker preserves that inconsistency (Results, paragraph 4, S6/P18).

S1-O3's reported values are exact: human minus GPT-3 on GPT-rated creativity β = .14, 95% CI [0.02, 0.25], t = 2.36, p = .02. The human-GPT-4 rating correlation r = .65 is also printed (Results, paragraphs 5-6, S6/P19-P20).

S1-O4's reported values are exact: GPT-4 versus human stories on GPT-rated creativity β = .76, 95% CI [0.60, 0.91], t = 9.74, p < .001. Its measure_detail also faithfully reproduces the pooled GPT-3 coefficient β = −.14, CI [−0.25, −0.02], t = 2.36, p = .02, including the source's positive t (Results, paragraph 7, S6/P21).

All numbers in one_line_finding match Results S6/P17-P18 and P21; its nonsignificance statements reproduce the authors' interpretation. These are regression differences in creativity ratings, not pooled standardized effects from a synthesis (Statistical Analyses S5/P14; Results S6).

DSI compares word embeddings within each story, so it is not diversity across different people's outputs under the codebook. The manuscript uses DSI and LIWC perceptual detail as predictors, with no randomized AI-assistance or post-AI outcome (Semantic Diversity S3/P12; Perceptual Details S4/P13; Statistical Analyses S5/P14).

This is an empirical report, so empty synthesis fields are appropriate. The XML includes no appendix and metadata says has-supplement = no. Funding is from the National Institute on Aging; conflicts are denied and data are available on request, with no public data/code URL stated (front metadata; back matter; S8/P27).
summary: The NIH author manuscript confirms an AI-versus-human output comparison, with no randomized assignment of people to AI assistance, and all reported effect numbers match the source. Corrections concern unsupported post-exclusion counts, standard-error availability, result locators, AI-availability coding, and the page count of the XML source.
